Laozi. Literally meaning Old Master, a legendary author traditionally credited with composing the Tao Te Ching, the foundational text of Taoism and philosophical Daoism. Living during the late Zhou Dynasty, with exact dates debated—possibly sixth to fifth century BCE—he is revered as a sage and spiritual patriarch in Chinese philosophy and religion. Though his historical existence remains contested by scholars, Laozi became one of the most influential philosophical voices in human history, shaping Eastern thought, martial arts, medicine, and aesthetics for over twenty-five hundred years.

His name means Old Master, and he may be a historical person, a composite figure, or a legendary projection. Traditional biography claims he was the court archivist of the Zhou dynasty and withdrew from society to write the Tao Te Ching. He is the reputed author of that text, also called the Daodejing or The Way and its Virtue, a cryptic, poetic text of eighty-one aphoristic chapters that became the philosophical cornerstone of Taoism and influenced all East Asian thought.

The Tao Te Ching teaches wu wei, or non-action and effortless action, the principle of flowing with the natural way of the universe rather than imposing force or will—a radical alternative to Confucius's emphasis on ritual, hierarchy, and moral cultivation. In religious Taoism, Laozi is deified as one of the Three Pure Ones, the highest deities in Taoism, and is depicted as an immortal sage who achieved enlightenment through spiritual practice and union with the Tao. He embodies the Taoist ideal of simplicity, humility, and withdrawal from the material world and political ambition, serving as a philosophical counterweight to Confucian engagement and social responsibility.

The Tao he describes is ineffable—"The Tao that can be spoken of is not the eternal Tao"—meaning reality transcends language, logic, and conceptual thought, requiring direct intuitive experience. His influence pervades Chinese literature, painting, calligraphy, and martial arts including kung fu and tai chi, and he merged with Buddhist thought to create Zen Buddhism, which spread throughout East Asia. The Zhuangzi, another foundational Taoist text written centuries after Laozi, centers on Laozi and deepens his philosophical legacy through dialogical storytelling.
